premise: Calibrating each gene against a null of the right shape stops the score measuring how many observations a gene had. It does nothing about the other half of the same problem: 17,916 genes are being ranked, and taking the top of 17,916 numbers is itself a selection operator. A z of 3 is unremarkable when you drew 17,916 of them.

assumption.claim: The calibrated z is standard normal, so the upper tail of N(0,1) is a p-value.
assumption.testedOn: the non-essential control genes, which should score at zero and are therefore an empirical null
assumption.whyItMatters: The first two moments pass and the shape does not: a mean of 0.036 and a standard deviation of 1.013 look like a textbook pass, and the distribution is still not normal. Reporting mean and sd alone would have declared this calibration correct.
assumption.verdict: FAILS: the controls depart from standard normal at the 1% level, so every parametric p-value below is wrong by an amount this test quantifies. The empirical column is the one to read.

empiricalResolution.says: An empirical p cannot go below 1/(1+726) = 1.38e-03 no matter how extreme the gene is, so this column cannot separate the very top of the list. That is a real limit of resampling against a finite control set, not a rounding choice.

naive.says: The threshold the shortlist has been using implicitly. Against 17916 genes, |z| > 3 is not a 0.1% error rate — it is 0.1% of 17,916, which is about eighteen false positives before anything real appears.

finding: The correction changes the size of the defensible list, not its top. What it buys is a statement no threshold can make: at a false discovery rate of 5%, this many genes, and of those roughly one in twenty is expected to be wrong. A cut at z > 3 says nothing about how many of the genes past it are noise.
